objectives.text: Keep the Cabo Delgado gas perimeter secure enough for the TotalEnergies-led LNG project to run. The full restart was announced on 29 January 2026, with first LNG expected in 2029, and the force that guards the site is Rwandan and, from 2026, paid for by Maputo (Kigali's claim).

means.text: Paid security. A Rwandan force of about 6,300 soldiers and police (Kigali's figure, April 2026) guards the LNG area, and EU-trained units under EUMAM-MOZ, led by Portugal, number about 2,000 Mozambican personnel in programmes. The EU's EUR 20m for the Rwandans lapsed in May 2026; Maputo now says it has secured the funding, a claim so far made by Kigali.

means.text: Gas as the bankable asset. The US Export-Import Bank board voted on 13 March 2025 to proceed with a loan of up to USD 4.7bn for the LNG project, after a four-year delay. constraints.text: Legitimacy and aid. The October 2024 result is contested; the inauguration in January 2025 drew protests and clashes after Mondlane's return from exile, and Mondlane is largely outside the national dialogue that is to report in November 2026. The regional force left in 2024 and US aid was cut sharply in 2025, so the gap is filled by paid partners.

paradoxes.text: Maputo buys its gas security from a force Washington has sanctioned. The US designated the Rwandan defence force on 2 March 2026, and Rwanda has threatened to stop protecting the US-financed gas project if its paid mission is not sustained. The security the state buys protects the export-credit project, and the same force is the one that puts that project at risk.

grand_strategy.reading: Mozambique is a state that sells its gas perimeter and rents its army. The LNG project, relaunched in 2026 with US export credit behind it, is the reason foreign forces stand in Cabo Delgado, and the Rwandan force is now paid for with money Maputo does not yet have, while it answers to Kigali. The IMF deal and the debt restructuring that follows will show whether the state can keep the gas and the paying partners after the EU money and the SADC force have left.

stances.note: Partner, warming: Maputo buys a security service from Kigali and does not treat Rwanda as an ally. The grade is our reading (C), not a source's word: Kigali's own account (Polity, 20 May 2026) says Mozambique has secured and will keep securing the money for the Rwandan force, after the EU's EUR 20m lapsed. Warming because the arrangement moved from EU-funded to Mozambique-funded in 2026. Bond none: a paid arrangement, with no kinship or affinity in the sources. Gap: no Mozambican official statement on the funding was read; the amount and term are undisclosed. Mirror: the RWA card's sources toward Mozambique, as evidence only; the grade is Maputo's own.

stances.note: Partner, with kinship as the bond: the Lusophone link (the CPLP and the 6th Luso-Mozambican summit in Porto) runs under a transactional military cooperation with Lisbon, not an alliance. Mozambique and Portugal jointly asked in 2026 to extend the EU training mission (EUMAM-MOZ) to 2028, which is the evidence for cooperation; the grade is our reading (C) and the bond is the Portuguese card's reading, mirrored because Maputo's own card holds no source for the bond. Trend stable. Gap: no Portuguese or Mozambican statement of the bond was read in 2026.

stances.note: Partner: trade, migration and the border, with no security alignment since the SADC mission ended. Not a quarrel: the SADC mission (SAMIM) withdrew in April to July 2024 for financial reasons, and South Africa's contingent (about 1,500 troops, Stratfor citing Zitamar) was among the first to leave. The official SADC statement is tier 1 for the start of the drawdown on 5 April 2024; the rest of the grade is our reading (B). Bond none: no kinship, affinity or grievance found in the sources. Gap: trade and migration figures were not read in this pass.

stances.note: Partner, transactional: the United States finances the LNG export (EXIM board, 13 March 2025, up to USD 4.7bn, official) and then cut its own aid sharply in 2025 (a US memo put it at nearly half of USAID's spending in Mozambique). The two pull in opposite directions, so the trend is stable and the grade is our reading (B), with the EXIM decision as the tier 1 anchor. Bond none: pure interest. Gap: the December 2025 US-Mozambique memorandum (a multi-year programme) was seen only as a search digest, with no source read, so it is not used here.

The Cabo Delgado insurgency and TotalEnergies' Mozambique LNG (full restart announced 29 Jan 2026, first LNG expected 2029) are the stakes; no Portuguese state financing or diplomatic role in the LNG project was found, only the private contractor Mota-Engil. stances_toward.note: Partner, warming: the clearest case of Rwanda selling security. The Rwandan force arrived in Cabo Delgado in July 2021, grew from 2,000 to about 6,300 (government spokeswoman; other press says 5,000 and over 2,000), and since the EU's EPF money ended in May 2026 Nduhungirehe says Mozambique has secured and will continue to secure the funding (amount and term undisclosed); a fresh contingent was briefed in Kigali on 30 Jul 2026. The deployment guards the TotalEnergies LNG area, which relaunched in January 2026. Not ally: the arrangement is a paid service, not an alignment, and Kigali showed (Mar 2026) that it would withdraw if unpaid. Bond none.

stances_toward.note: Partner in security, transactional: South African forces entered Cabo Delgado in mid-2021 under the SADC mission (SAMIM) and grew to about 1,500 troops, the largest contingent, funded mostly by Pretoria through the SADC Peace Fund. The presidential authorisation lapsed in April 2024, and the Mozambican government said in May 2024 that it knew of no plan for a South African force to stay. Trend stable: no later source on the relation. The Mozambique card is a stub, so there is no mirror. Confidence C: two tier 3 reports, and the troop figure comes from press reporting.
